# What planning buys: points {#sec-points}

```{r}
#| include: false
source("R/book.R")
```

Start with what already works, because it shows what is at stake.

A lazy array is cheap to hold and expensive to ask. Every question becomes
chunks to fetch, and for a remote store the cost is round trips. If R hands
over a whole question, the array can work out the distinct chunks it needs
and fetch them together. If R asks piece by piece, the array answers piece
by piece.

For points, R hands over the whole question. A matrix subscript,
`x[cbind(i, j, k)]`, is turned into linear positions and passed to the
ALTREP `Extract_subset` method in one call.

## The example

A synthetic array laid out like the Copernicus global waves store (chunks
of 4 x 8 cells, long in time), where each fetch call takes 50 ms. Three
hundred scattered points, read two ways.

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| eval: false
#| file: scripts/01-points.R
```

```{r}
res <- book_run("01-points.R")
book_table(res)
```

The two reads touch the same chunks. The matrix subscript is one batch; the
loop is one fetch call per chunk it had not seen yet. And the two builds of
R agree: nothing in this chapter needs the patch.

## On a real store

The same shape of read against the live Copernicus waves Zarr (1800 x 899
x 136,360 values of significant wave height, 3-hourly since 1980), run from
a workstation on 2026-11-13 with
[`examples/xyt-points`](https://github.com/mdsumner/r-variants/tree/main/examples/xyt-points):
300 points in the Southern Ocean were one fetch call for 268 chunks in 23
seconds at 8 connections, 15 seconds at 16 and 11 at 32. Done point by
point it is 268 round trips in series.

A layer-oriented reader can reach the same byte count, by grouping points
by chunk, reading each group as a slab and picking out each point's layer.
That is the planner written by hand. Here it is what `x[idx]` does.

## So what is missing

Points are the case R already gets right. The rest of the book is about
the reads next to it: a time series at a station, `x[i, j, ]`; a map,
`x[, , t]`; a box, `x[i0:i1, j0:j1, t0:t1]`. Those are the everyday
array reads, and they are the ones R takes apart.
